title: Venn Diagrams
summary: Two question families: (1) region arithmetic — count union, intersection, only-regions, exactly-two, neither using inclusion-exclusion over labelled Venn regions; (2) relation selection — decide whether categories nest (definitional necessity), stay apart (impossibility) or intersect (possible but not forced). The arithmetic family is pure formula discipline; the relation family is two quick tests per pair. Label every region before computing and both become near-90% accuracy topics.

subtopics.title: What a Venn diagram encodes
subtopics.concept: A Venn diagram is a picture of groups. Each circle is one group. Where two circles overlap, the members belong to both groups. First learn to read regions, then learn to add them.

formulas.name: Two-set union
formulas.note: The overlap is counted twice on the right, so subtract it once.

formulas.name: Only A
formulas.note: Only A is A minus the overlap.

formulas.name: Number of parts
formulas.note: n circles make 2 to the power n parts, including the outside.

tricks.title: Write numbers into the regions
tricks.body: Do not keep numbers in your head. Write each one in its region. The answer is then a single sum.

example.q: 60 students. 35 like tea, 30 like coffee, 10 like both. How many like neither?

tricks.title: Shade and compare
tricks.body: For a 'which expression' question, shade the phrase first. Then shade each option. Pick the match.

mistakes.wrong: Adding 35 (tea) and 30 (coffee) and calling it the number who like a drink.
mistakes.right: The overlap is counted twice. Subtract it once: 35 + 30 − 10 = 55.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'like tea' as 'like only tea'.
mistakes.right: 'Like tea' includes the overlap. 'Only tea' removes it.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the outside region.
mistakes.right: People who like neither drink sit outside both circles. Total minus union gives them.

mistakes.wrong: Counting three circles as 7 parts in all.
mistakes.right: There are 7 parts inside the circles and 1 outside, so 8 in all.

mistakes.wrong: Shading A ∪ B when the phrase says 'A and B'.
mistakes.right: 'And' means the overlap only. 'Or' means both circles together.

subtopics.notes:
### What a Venn diagram shows
A circle is a group of things. Everything inside the circle belongs to that group. Where two circles overlap, the things there belong to both groups.

Take two groups: people who like tea and people who like coffee. The picture has four parts.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Only tea | Likes tea, does not like coffee |
| Both | Likes tea and coffee |
| Only coffee | Likes coffee, does not like tea |
| Outside | Likes neither |

> **Rule:** Every person sits in exactly one part. No person is counted in two parts.

### Reading the region numbers
Numbers are written inside the parts. Add the parts you need and nothing more.

Suppose only-tea is 20, both is 15, only-coffee is 4 and outside is 10. The total is 20 + 15 + 4 + 10 = 49.

- People who like tea: 20 + 15 = 35. Tea includes the "both" part.
- People who like at least one drink: 20 + 15 + 4 = 39.
- People who like tea only: 20.

> **Watch:** "Likes tea" and "likes only tea" are not the same. The first one includes the overlap.

### Turning words into regions
Exam questions describe a region in words. You must find the matching part of the picture.

| Words | Region |
|---|---|
| A and B | The overlap of A and B |
| A or B | Both circles together |
| Only A | A, without the overlap |
| Not A | Everything outside circle A |
| Neither A nor B | Outside both circles |

For three sets, the words "A and B but not C" point to one small region. That is the overlap of A and B, with the part inside C removed.

> **Tip:** Draw the circles and shade the region for each option. The option with the same shading is the answer.

### How many regions are there
With one circle there are 2 parts: inside and outside. With two circles there are 4 parts. With three circles there are 8 parts.

The pattern is 2 multiplied by itself once for each circle. Three circles give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 parts. One part is outside all circles, so 7 parts are inside.

> **Note:** A drawing with three overlapping circles has 7 inside parts. Do not count the outside as a circle part.

### Words that need care
Some small words change the region. Read them slowly.

- "Neither A nor B" means outside both circles.
- "Exactly one" means only A plus only B. The overlap is left out.
- "At least one" means all the parts inside the circles.
- "Do not like A" means the total minus everyone in A.

Example: 100 people, and 56 like A. Then 100 − 56 = 44 do not like A.

> **Example:** In a group of 80, 30 like A, 25 like B and 10 like both. At least one: 30 + 25 − 10 = 45. Neither: 80 − 45 = 35.

patterns.name: Phrase to set expression
patterns.howToSpot: A phrase such as 'A and B but not C'. The options are written with ∩, ∪ and −.
steps: List the parts of the picture the phrase covers.
For each option, list the parts it covers.
Pick the option with exactly the same parts.
patterns.why: Two expressions mean the same only when they cover the same parts.

example.q: Which expression shows 'in A and B but not in C'?  (a) A ∩ B ∩ C  (b) (A ∩ B) − C  (c) (A ∪ B) − C  (d) A − (B ∪ C)
steps: The phrase is one part: inside A and B, outside C.
(a) is the centre part, inside C. Reject.
(b) is A and B with C removed. Match.

patterns.name: Reading region numbers
patterns.howToSpot: A picture with numbers in the parts. It asks for a group total or an 'only' count.
steps: Read which parts the question wants.
Check that the parts you added are not overlapping.
patterns.why: The parts never overlap, so their numbers add cleanly.

example.q: In a diagram of tea and coffee drinkers: only tea 20, both 15, only coffee 4, neither 10. How many like at least one drink?
steps: At least one = only tea + both + only coffee.

patterns.name: Counting regions
patterns.howToSpot: It asks how many parts or regions a diagram with 2 or 3 circles has.
steps: Subtract 1 if the outside is not counted.
patterns.why: Each member is inside or outside every circle, which gives 2 choices per circle.

example.q: How many separate parts (outside included) does a Venn diagram of 3 overlapping circles have?

patterns.name: Not and at most
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'do not', 'not in', or 'other than' a group.
steps: Find the members of the group.
Subtract the group from the total.
patterns.why: 'Not in A' is everything except A.

example.q: 100 people were asked. 56 like A. How many do not like A?

patterns.name: Neither, nor and exactly one
patterns.howToSpot: The words 'neither ... nor', 'exactly one' or 'only one' appear with two groups.
steps: Find the union: A + B − both.
For neither, subtract the union from the total.
For exactly one, subtract the overlap from the union.
patterns.why: Neither is outside the circles. Exactly one leaves out the overlap.

example.q: In a group of 80, 30 like A, 25 like B and 10 like both. How many like neither? How many like exactly one?

revision: Each circle is a group. The overlap is 'both'. The outside is 'neither'.
Two circles give 4 parts. Three circles give 8 parts, 7 of them inside.
'Likes A' includes the overlap. 'Only A' does not.
'Neither A nor B' means outside both circles.
At least one = total minus neither.
Fill numbers into the regions before you add.

subtopics.title: Two-circle counting
subtopics.concept: Two circles make four parts: only A, only B, both, and neither. Every two-circle question is a sum or a difference of these four parts. Fill them in, then read off the answer.

formulas.name: Two-set union
formulas.note: The overlap is counted twice on the right, so subtract it once.

formulas.name: Only A
formulas.note: Only A is A minus the overlap.

tricks.title: Add the four parts to check
tricks.body: After you fill only A, both, only B and neither, add them. If the sum is not the total, one part is wrong.

example.q: 150 families: 90 have a car, 70 have a two-wheeler, 40 have both. Check the parts.
steps: Only car 50, both 40, only two-wheeler 30, neither 30.
example.answer: The parts add to 150, so all are right.

tricks.title: Overlap limits
tricks.body: The overlap can never be more than the smaller group. It can never be less than A + B − total.

example.q: 100 people: 70 speak Hindi, 60 speak English. Find the smallest and largest overlap.

mistakes.wrong: Adding 90 + 70 and calling 160 the union.
mistakes.right: The overlap is counted twice. Union = 90 + 70 − 40 = 120.

mistakes.wrong: Treating 'both' as 'only both'.
mistakes.right: 'Both' is the overlap. 'Only A' removes it from A.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting to subtract the union from the total to get neither.
mistakes.right: Neither = total − union.

mistakes.wrong: Giving a negative number as the smallest overlap.
mistakes.right: If A + B − total is negative, the smallest overlap is 0.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing percent and headcount in one sum.
mistakes.right: Change all numbers to percent, or all to counts, first.

subtopics.notes:
### The four parts
Two groups A and B split everyone into four parts.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Only A | In A, not in B |
| Both | In A and in B |
| Only B | In B, not in A |
| Neither | In neither group |

Only A, both and only B together make the union. The union is "at least one". Neither is what is left of the total.

### The main formula
When you add A and B, the "both" part is counted twice. Subtract it once to fix that.

$$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$$

> **Rule:** Union = A + B − both. Neither = total − union.

Example: 150 families. 90 have a car, 70 have a two-wheeler, 40 have both. Union = 90 + 70 − 40 = 120. Neither = 150 − 120 = 30.

### Finding the only parts
"Only A" means A without the overlap. So only A = A − both.

In the same example, only car = 90 − 40 = 50. Only two-wheeler = 70 − 40 = 30. Check: 50 + 40 + 30 + 30 = 150.

> **Tip:** After you fill the four parts, add them. The sum must equal the total. This catches every slip.

### Working backwards
Sometimes the overlap is the unknown. Rearrange the main formula.

$$\text{both} = A + B - \text{union}$$

Example: 45 students. 28 play cricket, 22 play football, and each plays at least one. Union = 45. Both = 28 + 22 − 45 = 5.

### Percentages
Percent questions work the same way, with a total of 100.

Example: 60% like tea, 45% like coffee, and 15% like neither. Union = 100 − 15 = 85. Both = 60 + 45 − 85 = 20%.

> **Watch:** If the question gives a percent and a headcount, change everything to one form first.

### Biggest and smallest overlap
Sometimes the overlap is not given. You then find the smallest and the largest possible value.

- Largest overlap = the smaller of A and B. One group sits fully inside the other.
- Smallest overlap = A + B − total, or 0 if that is negative. The groups spread out as much as possible.

Example: 100 people. 70 speak Hindi and 60 speak English. Smallest both = 70 + 60 − 100 = 30. Largest both = 60.

> **Note:** A negative answer for the smallest overlap means the groups can be apart. Then the smallest overlap is 0.

### Reading the wording
Exam words hide the four parts. Turn each phrase into a part before you calculate.

| Phrase | Part |
|---|---|
| "at least one", "either or both" | Union |
| "both", "and" | Overlap |
| "only A", "A but not B" | A − both |
| "exactly one", "only one of the two" | Only A + only B |
| "neither", "none" | Total − union |

Example: 80 people. 50 read English news, 40 read Hindi news, 20 read both. Exactly one language = 50 + 40 − 2 × 20 = 50. Neither = 80 − (50 + 40 − 20) = 10.

patterns.name: Union and neither
patterns.howToSpot: Two group totals, their overlap and the size of the whole group. It asks for at least one, neither or only one.
patterns.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
patterns.why: The overlap is counted twice in A + B, so it is removed once.

example.q: Of 150 families, 90 have a car, 70 have a two-wheeler and 40 have both. How many have neither?

patterns.name: Find the overlap
patterns.howToSpot: The total and both group sizes are given. Everyone is in at least one group. It asks for the overlap.
steps: Write the union. If everyone is in a group, union = total.
patterns.why: The extra people in A + B over the union are exactly the overlap.

example.q: In a class of 45, 28 play cricket and 22 play football. Every student plays at least one. How many play both?

patterns.name: Percentages in two sets
patterns.howToSpot: The data are in percent. It asks for the percent in both or in neither.
patterns.why: Percent is a count out of 100, so the same formula works.

example.q: In a town, 60% like tea, 45% like coffee and 15% like neither. What percent like both?

patterns.name: Biggest and smallest overlap
patterns.howToSpot: The overlap is not given. It asks for the 'least' or 'greatest' possible number in both.
patterns.formula: Smallest = A + B − total; largest = smaller set
steps: Smallest overlap: A + B − total. Use 0 if negative.
Largest overlap: the smaller of A and B.
Any overlap between these two is possible.
patterns.why: The groups overlap least when spread apart, and most when one sits inside the other.

example.q: 100 people: 70 speak Hindi and 60 speak English. Find the least and the greatest number who speak both.

patterns.name: Exactly one group
patterns.howToSpot: The words 'only one of the two' or 'exactly one'. Only-A and only-B are added.
steps: Subtract the overlap from A to get only A.
Subtract the overlap from B to get only B.
patterns.why: The overlap is taken out of both groups, so it is subtracted twice.

example.q: 40 people like A, 30 like B and 12 like both. How many like exactly one of the two?

revision: Union = A + B − both.
Neither = total − union.
Only A = A − both.
Both = A + B − union.
Exactly one = A + B − 2 × both.
Largest overlap = the smaller set. Smallest overlap = A + B − total (not below 0).
Add the four parts at the end. They must equal the total.

subtopics.title: Three-circle counting
subtopics.concept: Three circles make eight parts: seven inside and one outside. The union formula adds the singles, subtracts the pairs and adds the triple back. Then 'exactly one', 'exactly two' and 'none' are simple sums.

formulas.name: Three-set union
formulas.note: Add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple back.

formulas.name: Exactly two
formulas.note: Sum of the pair figures minus three times the triple.

formulas.name: Exactly one
formulas.note: Remove the multi-group members from the union.

tricks.title: Strip the triple
tricks.body: For 'exactly two', take the pair numbers and remove the triple three times. It works because each pair holds the triple once.

example.q: AB = 8, BC = 7, AC = 6 and all three = 3. How many are in exactly two groups?

tricks.title: Fill the centre first
tricks.body: Start with the all-three part. Then fill the pairs, then the singles. Each step needs only the numbers you already have.

mistakes.wrong: Using the pair numbers as 'exactly two'.
mistakes.right: Each pair includes the triple. Exactly two = sum of pairs − 3 × triple.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting to add the triple back in the union formula.
mistakes.right: Union = singles − pairs + triple. The triple must be added once.

mistakes.wrong: Finding 'only A' as A − AB − AC without the triple.
mistakes.right: The triple is subtracted twice there. Add it back: A − AB − AC + ABC.

mistakes.wrong: Taking the union as the final answer for 'none'.
mistakes.right: None = total − union.

mistakes.wrong: Not checking for a negative part.
mistakes.right: Every part must be 0 or more. A negative part means a slip.

subtopics.notes:
### The seven parts
Three groups A, B and C make seven parts inside the circles.

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Only A, only B, only C | In one group only |
| A and B only, B and C only, A and C only | In exactly two groups |
| All three | In A, B and C |

The outside is the eighth part. It holds people in none of the groups.

### Why the union formula works
Add the three groups first. People in two groups are counted twice. People in all three are counted three times.

Subtract the three pairs. Now the all-three people are counted 3 − 3 = 0 times. Add the all-three part back once.

$$n(A \cup B \cup C) = \Sigma A - \Sigma \text{pairs} + \text{triple}$$

> **Rule:** Union = (A + B + C) − (AB + BC + AC) + ABC. None = total − union.

### Worked example
There are 60 members. A has 30, B has 25 and C has 20. The pairs are 10, 8 and 7. All three is 4.

Union = 75 − 25 + 4 = 54. None = 60 − 54 = 6.

> **Tip:** Write the seven numbers in a list before you start. This stops missed terms.

### Filling the parts from the outside in
The pair numbers include the centre part. So remove the triple from each pair before you use it.

- Only A and B = AB − ABC.
- Only A = A − (AB − ABC) − (AC − ABC) − ABC, which equals A − AB − AC + ABC.

Example: A = 45, AB = 15, AC = 12, ABC = 6. Only A = 45 − 15 − 12 + 6 = 24.

### Exactly one, two or three
Each pair figure contains the triple once. So the three pair figures together contain it three times.

- Exactly two = AB + BC + AC − 3 × ABC.
- At least two = AB + BC + AC − 2 × ABC.
- Exactly one = union − exactly two − ABC.

> **Watch:** "Exactly two" is not the sum of the pairs. That sum has the triple counted three times.

Example: pairs 14, 12 and 11, and triple 5. Exactly two = 37 − 15 = 22.

### Working backwards
Sometimes the union is given and a group total is missing. Rearrange the formula.

$$\Sigma A = \text{union} + \Sigma \text{pairs} - \text{triple}$$

Example: union 120, pairs add to 50, triple 20. Then A + B + C = 120 + 50 − 20 = 150.

> **Note:** After you find every part, check that no part is negative. A negative part means a number was misread.

### Full check on the club example
Use the 60-member club again: A = 30, B = 25, C = 20, pairs 10, 8, 7, triple 4.

- Only A = 30 − 10 − 7 + 4 = 17. Only B = 25 − 10 − 8 + 4 = 11. Only C = 20 − 8 − 7 + 4 = 9.
- Exactly one = 17 + 11 + 9 = 37.
- Exactly two = 25 − 3 × 4 = 13.
- All three = 4, and none = 6.

Add them: 37 + 13 + 4 + 6 = 60. The parts match the total, so every step was right.

patterns.name: Union and none
patterns.howToSpot: Three group totals, three pair overlaps and the triple. It asks for at least one or for none.
patterns.formula: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = ΣA − Σpairs + triple
steps: For none, subtract the union from the total.
patterns.why: The triple is added 3 times and taken out 3 times, so add it back once.

example.q: There are 60 members. A has 30, B has 25, C has 20. The pairs are 10, 8 and 7, and all three is 4. How many are in none?

patterns.name: Exactly two groups
patterns.howToSpot: The words 'exactly two' or 'only two' with three pair figures and the triple.
steps: Check with the parts if you have time.
patterns.why: Each pair figure includes the triple once, so the sum has it three times.

example.q: In a survey of three groups, the pair overlaps are 14, 12 and 11, and 5 are in all three. How many are in exactly two groups?

patterns.name: Find one region
patterns.howToSpot: It asks for 'only A' with A, the two pairs that include A, and the triple.
patterns.formula: Only A = A − AB − AC + ABC
patterns.why: AB and AC both include the triple, so it was subtracted twice.

example.q: A has 45 members. A and B share 15, A and C share 12, and 6 are in all three. How many are only in A?

patterns.name: Find the total of the groups
patterns.howToSpot: The union, the pair figures and the triple are given. It asks for the sum of the three groups.
patterns.why: The union formula is just rearranged.

example.q: The union of three groups is 120. The pairs add up to 50 and the triple is 20. What is A + B + C?

patterns.name: Exactly one group
patterns.howToSpot: It asks for members in only one of the three groups.
patterns.formula: Exactly one = union − exactly two − triple
steps: Subtract exactly two and the triple from the union.
patterns.why: The union is split into exactly one, exactly two and all three.

example.q: For groups with A = 30, B = 25, C = 20, pairs 10, 8, 7 and triple 4, how many are in exactly one group?

patterns.name: At least two groups
patterns.howToSpot: The words 'two or more groups' or 'at least two'.
steps: This equals exactly two plus the triple.
patterns.why: Exactly two is the pairs minus 3 triples. At least two adds the triple back once.

example.q: The pair overlaps are 14, 12 and 11, and 5 are in all three. How many are in at least two groups?

revision: Union = A + B + C − AB − BC − AC + ABC.
None = total − union.
Only A = A − AB − AC + ABC.
Exactly two = AB + BC + AC − 3 × ABC.
At least two = AB + BC + AC − 2 × ABC.
Exactly one = union − exactly two − ABC.
A + B + C = union + pairs − triple.
Every part must be 0 or more.

subtopics.title: Choosing the correct diagram
subtopics.concept: Some questions give three words and ask which picture shows them. Judge each pair of words on its own. The pair is nested, overlapping or separate. The correct picture agrees on every pair.

tricks.title: One pair at a time
tricks.body: Never judge the whole picture at once. Decide each pair, then pick the option that agrees with all three pairs.

example.q: Mothers, Females, Engineers. Which picture fits?
steps: Mothers and Females: every mother is a female, so nested.
Engineers and Females: male engineers exist, women engineers exist, so crossing.
Pick the picture with a small circle inside Females and a crossing Engineers circle.
example.answer: Mothers inside Females, Engineers crossing both

tricks.title: Big class first
tricks.body: Find the widest word first. Draw it as the big circle. Then place the other words inside, across, or outside it.

mistakes.wrong: Drawing engineers inside females because you thought of women engineers.
mistakes.right: Male engineers exist too. So engineers cross females, and are not inside.

mistakes.wrong: Making two types, like cats and dogs, overlap.
mistakes.right: No cat is a dog. Draw two separate circles inside the class.

mistakes.wrong: Judging the whole picture at once.
mistakes.right: Check one pair at a time. Drop an option as soon as one pair is wrong.

mistakes.wrong: Nesting words that only sometimes belong together.
mistakes.right: Nest only when every X is a Y. Otherwise draw crossing circles.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the class circle for two types.
mistakes.right: Cats and dogs both sit inside animals. Draw the big circle.

subtopics.notes:
### The three ways two words can relate
Take two words X and Y. Ask if every X is a Y, and if any X can be a Y.

| Relation | Test | Picture |
|---|---|---|
| Nested | Every X is a Y | X circle inside Y circle |
| Overlapping | Some X can be Y, not all | Two circles that cross |
| Separate | No X can be Y | Two circles apart |

> **Rule:** Ask two questions. Is every X a Y? Can any X be a Y? The answers give the picture.

### Nested words
A type sits inside its class. Every sparrow is a bird, and every bird is an animal.

So Sparrows, Birds and Animals make three circles, one inside the next. A part of a part is a part of the whole.

> **Tip:** Go from the smallest word to the largest. Each word must fit inside the next.

### Two types inside one class
Cats and dogs are both animals. But no cat is a dog.

So there is one big circle for Animals. Inside it are two separate small circles, Cats and Dogs. The small circles do not touch.

### Words that cross
Some words share members but neither fits inside the other. Doctors, Women and Teachers are like this.

A woman can be a doctor. A doctor can be a teacher. But not every doctor is a woman. So each pair crosses, and you draw three crossing circles.

> **Watch:** Do not put engineers inside females because you can think of women engineers. Male engineers also exist.

### Mixed pictures
Some sets are a mix. Take Mothers, Females and Engineers.

Every mother is a female, so Mothers sit inside Females. Engineers can be female or male, and can be mothers or not. So Engineers cross both circles.

### Unrelated words
Pens, Books and Tables have nothing in common. No pen is a book, and no book is a table.

So the picture is three circles that do not touch. Boys and Girls are also separate, with both inside Students.

> **Note:** When one pair is wrong in an option, the whole option is wrong. Test the options pair by pair and drop the first one that fails.

### Common word sets
Exams repeat a few word sets. Learn the picture for each.

| Words | Picture |
|---|---|
| Surgeons, Doctors, Humans | Nested, one inside the next |
| Delhi, India, Asia | Nested, one inside the next |
| Pens, Pencils, Stationery | Two separate circles inside one big circle |
| Lawyers, Teachers, Women | Three crossing circles |
| Mothers, Females, Engineers | Mothers inside Females, Engineers crossing both |
| Pens, Books, Tables | Three separate circles |

> **Tip:** Decide the picture for each set before you look at the options. Then match the option.

patterns.name: Nested chain
patterns.howToSpot: Each word is a type of the next word: sparrow, bird, animal.
steps: Check that every X is a Y.
Check that every Y is a Z.
Draw the circles one inside the next.
patterns.why: A part of a part is a part of the whole.

example.q: Which picture shows Sparrows, Birds, Animals?
steps: Draw three circles, one inside the next.
example.answer: Three circles, one inside the next

patterns.name: Two subsets in a bigger set
patterns.howToSpot: Two words are types of a third word, and the two are different from each other.
steps: Find the widest word. Draw it as the big circle.
Check that the two other words cannot overlap.
Draw two separate circles inside the big one.
patterns.why: Both are inside the class, and no member is in both.

example.q: Which picture shows Cats, Dogs, Animals?
steps: Draw two separate circles inside one big circle.
example.answer: Two separate circles inside a big circle

patterns.name: Partial overlaps
patterns.howToSpot: The words are jobs or traits that a person can have together, with none forced.
steps: Ask if every X is a Y. If not, they are not nested.
Ask if some X can be a Y. If yes, they cross.
patterns.why: If members can be shared but are not forced, the circles cross.

example.q: Which picture shows Doctors, Women, Teachers?
steps: A doctor can be a woman, but not every doctor is.
A woman can be a teacher, but not every woman is.
A doctor can be a teacher, but not every doctor is.

patterns.name: Mixed: inside and crossing
patterns.howToSpot: One pair is nested and a third word crosses the nested pair.
steps: Find the pair with 'every X is a Y'. Nest it.
Test the third word against each of the two.
Draw it crossing the circles it overlaps.
patterns.why: Different pairs can have different relations in one picture.

example.q: Which picture shows Mothers, Females, Engineers?
steps: Every mother is a female: Mothers inside Females.
Engineers can be female or male: they cross Females.
Engineers can be mothers or not: they cross Mothers.
example.answer: Mothers inside Females, Engineers crossing both

patterns.name: Unrelated words
patterns.howToSpot: Three words have no link, such as objects of different kinds.
steps: Ask if any member of one word can be in another.
If no, the circles are separate.
patterns.why: No shared member means no overlap.

example.q: Which picture shows Pens, Books, Tables?

revision: Ask: is every X a Y? Can some X be a Y?
Every X is a Y: X circle inside Y circle.
Some X can be Y, not all: crossing circles.
No X can be Y: separate circles.
Two types of one class: two separate circles inside the big circle.
Test pair by pair. One wrong pair removes the option.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two totals and the overlap; asks at least one, only one or neither.
pyqPatterns.approach: Union = A + B − both; neither = total − union; only A = A − both.

example.q: In a class of 60, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 10 like both. How many like neither?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Some regions are given; the overlap, a circle total or the group size is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Draw four boxes (only A, only B, both, neither), fill the known ones and solve for the gap.

example.q: Everyone in a class of 80 plays chess or carrom; 50 play chess and 40 carrom. How many play both?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Data in percent, answer in percent or in people.
pyqPatterns.approach: Solve in percent with total 100, convert to people at the end.

example.q: 70% watch cricket, 60% football, 40% both. What percent watch neither?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Overlap not given; asks its largest or smallest possible value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Max both = smaller set; min both = A + B − N (not below 0); max neither = N − larger set.

example.q: 80 people; 50 like cricket, 40 hockey. Maximum who like neither?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three totals, three pairs, the triple and a group size.
pyqPatterns.approach: Union = ΣA − Σpairs + triple; none = total − union.

example.q: 200 people: coffee 90, tea 80, milk 70; pairs 40, 35, 30; all three 15. How many drink none?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Asks for exactly one, exactly two or at least two sets.
pyqPatterns.approach: Exactly two = Σpairs − 3 × triple; at least two = Σpairs − 2 × triple; exactly one = union − exactly two − triple.

example.q: Pairs 8, 7, 6 and all three 3. Exactly two?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Numbers are written in each region; the question describes a group in words.
pyqPatterns.approach: List the regions the phrase covers and add them once each; use total − regions for 'not' phrases.

example.q: Only N 20, only T 25, only R 5, N-T 15, T-R 6, N-R 4, all 10. How many use exactly one source?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three words; options describe circle pictures.
pyqPatterns.approach: For each pair decide inside / apart / cross by definition, then match all three marks to one picture.

example.q: Even numbers, Odd numbers, Prime numbers.
example.solution: Even and odd never meet; 2 and 3 are prime → **two separate circles, with the third intersecting both**.

solvedExamples.q: In a class of **60 students, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 10 like both.** How many students like **neither** tea nor coffee?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add both counts, subtract the overlap once, subtract from the total.

solvedExamples.q: In a survey, **8 people read A and B, 7 read B and C, 6 read A and C, and 3 read all three.** How many read **exactly two** papers?
solvedExamples.solution: (8 − 3) + (7 − 3) + (6 − 3) = **12**. Each pairwise figure wrongly includes the triple readers.

solvedExamples.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Doctors, Men and Writers**?
options: Three completely separate circles
Doctors and Writers both inside the Men circle
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Doctors inside Men; Writers a separate circle
solvedExamples.solution: No category is definitionally inside another (a doctor need not be a man; men need not write), and none is impossible to combine. So all three circles pairwise intersect.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Run necessity (nesting) and impossibility (separation) tests pair by pair; neither applies here.

solvedExamples.q: Of **200 people, 90 drink coffee, 80 tea, 70 milk; 40 coffee and tea, 35 tea and milk, 30 coffee and milk; 15 all three.** How many drink **none**?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add singles, subtract pairs, re-add triple, subtract from total.

practice.q: In a group, **|A ∪ B| = 40**, the number of elements in **A only is 15** and in **B only is 12**. How many elements are in **both A and B**?
practice.solution: Union = only-A + only-B + both → 40 = 15 + 12 + both → both = **13**.
practice.shortcut: The three inside-regions sum to the union.

practice.q: In a school, **40 students play hockey, 25 play cricket and 12 play both.** How many students play **hockey or cricket** (at least one)?
practice.shortcut: Singles minus overlap.

practice.q: In a survey, **70% of people watch cricket, 60% watch football and 40% watch both.** What percentage watch **neither**?
practice.shortcut: Percentages behave exactly like counts — total is 100.

practice.q: In a class of **80 students, every student plays at least one of chess and carrom. 50 play chess and 40 play carrom.** How many play **both**?
practice.solution: At least one = 80 → 50 + 40 − both = 80 → both = **10**.
practice.shortcut: 'Everyone plays' pins the union equal to the class strength.
Sum, subtract pairs, re-add the triple.

practice.q: In a colony of newspaper readers, **45 people read the Herald, 25 read both the Herald and the Tribune.** How many read **only the Herald**?
practice.solution: Only Herald = 45 − 25 = **20**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only X' = X minus the overlap.

practice.q: A club's three sports sections show: **15 members in badminton only, 10 in tennis only, 8 in chess only, 6 in badminton and tennis only, 5 in tennis and chess only, 4 in badminton and chess only, and 2 in all three.** How many members play **at least one** of the three sports?
practice.solution: The seven regions are disjoint — add them: 15+10+8+6+5+4+2 = **50**.
practice.shortcut: When every region is given 'only'-style, no formula — just add.

practice.q: Given **|A| = 22, |B| = 19, |C| = 17, |A∩B| = 9, |B∩C| = 7, |A∩C| = 6, |A∩B∩C| = 4** — how many elements belong to **exactly one** set?
practice.solution: Exactly two = (9−4)+(7−4)+(6−4) = 10. Exactly one = union − exactly two − triple = 40 − 10 − 4 = **26**.
practice.shortcut: Union minus everyone in two or three sets.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Squares, Rectangles and Polygons**?
options: Squares inside Rectangles, both inside Polygons
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Squares and Rectangles intersecting, both inside Polygons
Three completely separate circles
practice.solution: Every square is a rectangle and every rectangle is a polygon — a fully nested chain of circles.
practice.shortcut: Necessity test passes for every pair → nested circles.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Mothers, Females and Engineers**?
options: Mothers and Engineers inside Females
Engineers inside Females; Mothers separate
Mothers inside Females; Engineers circle intersecting both
All three circles intersecting equally
practice.solution: Every mother is definitionally a female → Mothers inside Females. Engineers can be male or female and may or may not be mothers → the Engineers circle crosses both.
practice.shortcut: Definition decides nesting; possibility decides intersection.

practice.q: **|A ∩ B| = 8, |A − B| = 10, |B| = 20 and 7 elements belong to neither set.** What is the size of the **universal set** (all elements considered)?
practice.shortcut: Four disjoint regions: both, A-only, B-only, neither.

practice.q: **|A| = 25, |B| = 20 and |A ∩ B| = 8.** How many elements are in **exactly one** of A and B?
practice.shortcut: Strip the lens from each circle and add the moons.

practice.q: In a batch of **120 trainees: 55 know Python, 45 know Java, 40 know C++; 20 know Python and Java, 18 know Java and C++, 15 know Python and C++; 8 know all three.** How many trainees know **none** of the three?
practice.shortcut: Full inclusion-exclusion, then subtract from the batch.

practice.q: **|A∩B| = 12, |B∩C| = 10, |A∩C| = 9 and |A∩B∩C| = 5.** How many elements belong to **at least two** of the sets?
practice.solution: At least two = exactly two + all three = (12−5)+(10−5)+(9−5) + 5 = 7+5+4+5 = **21**. Shortcut: pairwise sum 31 counts the triple 3 times → 31 − 2×5 = 21.
practice.shortcut: Pairwise sum − 2 × triple = at-least-two.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Words, English words and Hindi words**?
options: Three circles, each pair intersecting
English words inside Words; Hindi words a separate circle outside
All three nested inside one another
English and Hindi circles inside Words, not overlapping each other
practice.solution: Both are subsets of Words (necessity), and a word cannot be English and Hindi at once (impossibility) → two disjoint circles inside the big one.
practice.shortcut: One pair needs the impossibility test — the other two are simple nestings.

practice.q: In a three-circle diagram of Doctors (D), Singers (S) and Players (P), which expression shows the people who are **doctors and singers but not players**?
options: D ∩ S ∩ P
(D ∩ S) − P
D ∩ S
(D ∪ S) − P
practice.solution: The phrase needs D and S together, with P removed: **(D ∩ S) − P**, the single D-S-only region. D ∩ S alone also contains the all-three region; D ∩ S ∩ P is only the all-three region; (D ∪ S) − P also includes people who are only doctors or only singers.
practice.shortcut: 'And' → ∩, 'but not' → −. Check whether the all-three region sneaks in.

practice.q: Which expression shows the elements that belong to **exactly one of A and B**?
options: A ∪ B
A − B
A ∩ B
practice.solution: Exactly one = in A or B, but not in both: **(A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B)**, which is only A + only B. A ∪ B also includes the overlap; A ∩ B is the overlap itself; A − B misses the only-B part.
practice.shortcut: Exactly one = union minus overlap.

practice.q: Which expression shows the elements that are **in C but in neither A nor B**?
options: C − (A ∩ B)
C − A
C − (A ∪ B)
(A ∪ B) − C
practice.solution: 'Neither A nor B' means outside A **and** outside B, i.e. outside A ∪ B. So the set is **C − (A ∪ B)** = only C. C − (A ∩ B) wrongly keeps C-elements that are in just one of A, B; C − A still keeps the B-C-only region; (A ∪ B) − C is the opposite region.
practice.shortcut: Neither A nor B = remove the union, not the overlap.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use **at least two** of the three sources?
practice.solution: At least two = the three exactly-two regions + all three = 15 + 6 + 4 + 10 = **35**. 25 misses the all-three region; 45 wrongly adds the 'none' group.
practice.shortcut: At least two = exactly-two regions + centre.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people **read the newspaper** (with or without other sources)?
practice.solution: All four regions inside N: only N 20 + N-T 15 + N-R 4 + all three 10 = **49**. 20 is only-N; 39 forgets the all-three region.
practice.shortcut: A whole circle = its 4 regions.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use the **newspaper or the radio but not TV**?
practice.solution: Regions in N or R and outside T: only N 20 + only R 5 + N-R only 4 = **29**. 25 forgets the N-R region; 39 wrongly adds the all-three region, which contains TV watchers.
practice.shortcut: Remove every region that touches T.

practice.q: Three circles are drawn so that every pair overlaps and there is a region common to all three. Counting the space outside all circles, how many separate **regions** does the diagram have?
practice.solution: Each region is a yes/no choice for each circle: 2 × 2 × 2 = **8** (7 inside the circles + 1 outside). 7 forgets the outside region.
practice.shortcut: n circles → 2ⁿ regions including outside.

practice.q: In a standard diagram of three mutually intersecting circles A, B and C, **how many regions** together make up circle A?
practice.solution: Circle A is split by B and C into: only A, A-B only, A-C only and all three = **4** regions. 1 is only A; 3 forgets the centre.
practice.shortcut: A region inside A is a yes/no choice for B and C: 2 × 2 = 4.

practice.q: Two intersecting circles are drawn inside a rectangle that stands for the universal set. How many separate **regions** does the picture have?
practice.solution: Only A, only B, both, and the part of the rectangle outside both circles = **4**. 3 forgets the outside region.
practice.shortcut: Two circles → 2² = 4 regions.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use **exactly one** source?
practice.solution: Exactly one = only N + only T + only R = 20 + 25 + 5 = **50**. 65 wrongly adds the 15 who use none; 35 is the at-least-two count.
practice.shortcut: Exactly one = the three 'only' regions.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people **do not watch TV**?
practice.solution: TV regions = 25 + 15 + 6 + 10 = 56, so not TV = 100 − 56 = **44**. 75 subtracts only the 'only T' region; 29 forgets the 15 who use nothing.
practice.shortcut: Not T = total − whole T circle (the none group stays in).

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use **at most one** of the three sources?
practice.solution: At most one = exactly one + none = 50 + 15 = **65**. 50 forgets that zero sources is also 'at most one'; 35 is the at-least-two count.
practice.shortcut: At most one = total − at least two = 100 − 35.

practice.q: In a housing society of **150 families, 90 have a car, 70 have a two-wheeler and 40 have both**. How many families have **neither**?
practice.solution: At least one = 90 + 70 − 40 = 120. Neither = 150 − 120 = **30**. 70 comes from 150 − (50 + 30), which forgets the 40 families who have both.
practice.shortcut: Neither = total − (A + B − both).

practice.q: Of **250 employees, 140 speak Hindi, 120 speak Telugu and 30 speak neither**. How many speak **only Telugu**?
practice.solution: At least one = 250 − 30 = 220. Both = 140 + 120 − 220 = 40. Only Telugu = 120 − 40 = **80**. 40 is the 'both' figure; 100 is only Hindi.
practice.shortcut: Find both first, then subtract it from the circle.

practice.q: In a group, **30 people like mango, 15 like only guava, 12 like both mango and guava, and 8 like neither**. How many people are in the group?
practice.solution: The 30 mango-lovers already include the 12 who like both. Group = mango 30 + only guava 15 + neither 8 = **53**. 65 adds the 12 a second time.
practice.shortcut: Check whether a given figure is a whole circle or an 'only' region.

practice.q: In a class of **46 students, 10 play both cricket and football and 6 play neither**. The number who play **only cricket is twice** the number who play only football. How many play **cricket**?
practice.solution: Only C + only F = 46 − 6 − 10 = 30, with only C = 2 × only F → only F = 10, only C = 20. Cricket = only C + both = 20 + 10 = **30**. 20 is only cricket.
practice.shortcut: Fill the four boxes; the ratio splits the 'only' total.

practice.q: In a town, **65% of adults read a Hindi paper, 40% read an English paper and 20% read both**. If **3,000 adults read neither**, how many adults are there in the town?
practice.shortcut: Find the percent of the known group, then scale up.

practice.q: In an examination, **35% of candidates failed in Mathematics, 25% failed in English and 10% failed in both**. If **250 candidates passed in both** subjects, how many candidates appeared?
practice.solution: Failed at least one = 35 + 25 − 10 = 50%, so passed both = 50%. Total = 250 × 100 ÷ 50 = **500**. 625 comes from 100 − 35 − 25 = 40%, which forgets to add back the 10% who failed both.
practice.shortcut: Passed both = 100 − (fail₁ + fail₂ − fail both).

practice.q: In a class of **60 students, 45 like tea and 35 like coffee**. What is the **minimum** number of students who like both?
practice.solution: The circles can be pushed apart only until they fill the class: 45 + 35 − 60 = **20** must overlap. 35 is the *maximum* (coffee fully inside tea); 0 is impossible because 45 + 35 > 60.
practice.shortcut: Min both = A + B − N (not below 0).

practice.q: In a group of **80 people, 50 like cricket and 40 like hockey**. What is the **maximum** number of people who like **neither** game?
practice.solution: Neither is largest when the circles cover as few people as possible — hockey fully inside cricket. Then at least one = 50 and neither = 80 − 50 = **30**. 0 is the minimum; 10 is the minimum overlap.
practice.shortcut: Max neither = N − larger set.

practice.q: A sports club has **60 members: 30 play cricket, 25 play football and 20 play hockey; 10 play cricket and football, 8 play football and hockey, 7 play cricket and hockey, and 4 play all three**. How many members play **none** of the three?
practice.solution: Union = 30 + 25 + 20 − 10 − 8 − 7 + 4 = 54. None = 60 − 54 = **6**. 10 comes from forgetting to add back the 4 who play all three.
practice.shortcut: Union = ΣA − Σpairs + triple.

practice.q: In a survey, **50% of people like Hindi songs, 40% like Tamil songs and 30% like Punjabi songs; 20% like Hindi and Tamil, 15% like Tamil and Punjabi, 10% like Hindi and Punjabi, and 5% like all three**. What percentage like **none** of the three?
practice.shortcut: Percent data works exactly like counts.

practice.q: For three sets, **|A ∩ B| = 15, |B ∩ C| = 12, |A ∩ C| = 10 and |A ∩ B ∩ C| = 5**. How many elements belong to **exactly two** of the sets?
practice.solution: Each pairwise figure contains the triple once: (15 − 5) + (12 − 5) + (10 − 5) = 10 + 7 + 5 = **22**. 37 is the raw pairwise sum; 27 is 'at least two' (22 + 5).
practice.shortcut: Exactly two = Σpairs − 3 × triple.

practice.q: In a school club of **70 students, 30 take Music, 28 take Dance and 25 take Drama; 12 take Music and Dance, 10 take Dance and Drama, 9 take Music and Drama, and 4 take all three**. How many take **exactly one** activity?
practice.solution: Only Music = 30 − 12 − 9 + 4 = 13; only Dance = 28 − 12 − 10 + 4 = 10; only Drama = 25 − 10 − 9 + 4 = 10. Exactly one = **33**. 56 is the union; 19 is exactly two.
practice.shortcut: Exactly one = union − exactly two − triple = 56 − 19 − 4.

practice.q: For three sets, **|A| = 45, |A ∩ B| = 15, |A ∩ C| = 12 and |A ∩ B ∩ C| = 6**. How many elements are in **only A**?
practice.solution: Only A = 45 − 15 − 12 + 6 = **24**. Subtracting both pairs removes the triple twice, so it is added back once; 18 forgets that.
practice.shortcut: Only A = A − AB − AC + ABC.

practice.q: In an office, **40 people speak Kannada; 18 speak Kannada and Hindi, 15 speak Kannada and Tamil, and 7 speak all three languages**. How many speak **only Kannada**?
practice.solution: Only Kannada = 40 − 18 − 15 + 7 = **14**. 7 forgets to add back the 7 who were subtracted twice; 22 subtracts only the Hindi overlap.
practice.shortcut: Subtract both pairs, add the triple back once.

practice.q: For three sets, **|A| = 25, |B| = 30, |C| = 20, |A ∩ B| = 10, |B ∩ C| = 8, |A ∩ C| = 7** and **|A ∪ B ∪ C| = 55**. How many elements are in **all three** sets?
practice.solution: 55 = 25 + 30 + 20 − 10 − 8 − 7 + x = 50 + x → x = **5**. Check: only A = 13, only B = 17, only C = 10 — no region is negative.
practice.shortcut: Rearrange the master formula for the missing term.

practice.q: Each of **100 people reads at least one of three magazines. 60 read exactly one and 30 read exactly two**. What is the **sum of the readerships** of the three magazines?
practice.solution: All three = 100 − 60 − 30 = 10. A reader of two magazines is counted twice and a reader of three is counted three times: 60 + 2 × 30 + 3 × 10 = **150**. 100 counts each person once.
practice.shortcut: ΣA = exactly one + 2 × exactly two + 3 × all three.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Natural numbers, Whole numbers and Integers**?
options: Two separate circles inside a third circle
Three circles, each pair intersecting
One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
Three nested circles, one inside the next
practice.solution: Every natural number (1, 2, 3, …) is a whole number, and every whole number (0, 1, 2, …) is an integer → **three nested circles**.
practice.shortcut: Each word is a type of the next → nested.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Sparrows, Birds and Animals**?
options: Three nested circles, one inside the next
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Two separate circles inside a third circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
practice.solution: Every sparrow is a bird and every bird is an animal → **three nested circles**.
practice.shortcut: Type of a type → nested chain.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Pens, Pencils and Stationery**?
options: Three nested circles, one inside the next
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
Three completely separate circles
Two separate circles inside a third circle
practice.solution: Pens and pencils are both stationery, but nothing is both a pen and a pencil → **two separate circles inside a third**.
practice.shortcut: Two kinds of one thing that cannot overlap.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Whales, Mammals and Fish**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
Two separate circles inside a third circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Three nested circles, one inside the next
practice.solution: Every whale is a mammal. No fish is a mammal, so fish share nothing with mammals or whales → **one circle inside a second; the third separate from both**.
practice.shortcut: Test the third word against both circles.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Even numbers, Multiples of 3 and Integers**?
options: Two separate circles inside a third circle
Two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part
Three nested circles, one inside the next
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
practice.solution: Both are sets of integers. 6 is even and a multiple of 3, 4 is only even, 9 is only a multiple of 3 → they intersect. So **two intersecting circles inside a third**.
practice.shortcut: Two subsets of the big set — check whether they share members (6 does).

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Teachers, Women and Singers**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Three completely separate circles
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
practice.solution: A teacher may or may not be a woman or a singer, and a woman may or may not sing; all three can meet in one person → **three circles, each pair intersecting**.
practice.shortcut: No word is a type of another and every pair can share → all intersect.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Women, Engineers and Rivers**?
options: Three completely separate circles
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
Two intersecting circles and a third separate circle
practice.solution: Some women are engineers → those two intersect. A river is neither a woman nor an engineer → **two intersecting circles and a third separate circle**.
practice.shortcut: Decide each pair; a non-person category stands apart.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Even numbers, Odd numbers and Prime numbers**?
options: Two separate circles inside a third circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
Three circles, each pair intersecting
practice.solution: No number is both even and odd → separate. 2 is even and prime, 3 is odd and prime, while 4 and 9 are not prime → the Prime circle cuts both. Answer: **two separate circles, with the third intersecting both**.
practice.shortcut: Test with 2, 3, 4, 9.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Fathers, Men and Doctors**?
options: Three circles, each pair intersecting
One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting only the outer circle
practice.solution: Every father is a man → Fathers inside Men. Some fathers are doctors and some are not; some men are doctors → the Doctors circle crosses both. Answer: **one circle inside a second; the third intersecting both**.
practice.shortcut: Draw the subset first, then test the third word against inner and outer.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Multiples of 4, Multiples of 2 and Multiples of 3**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
Two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part
practice.solution: Every multiple of 4 is a multiple of 2 → inside. 12 is a multiple of 4 (and 2) and of 3; 6 is a multiple of 2 and 3 but not 4; 9 is a multiple of 3 only → the third circle crosses both. Answer: **one circle inside a second; the third intersecting both**.
practice.shortcut: Check 12, 6 and 9.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Multiples of 5, Multiples of 7 and Multiples of 35**?
options: Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
Three nested circles, one inside the next
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
Two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part
practice.solution: 35 = 5 × 7, so every multiple of 35 is a multiple of both 5 and 7. Multiples of 5 and 7 overlap (35, 70) but neither contains the other (10, 14). Answer: **two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part**.
practice.shortcut: A common multiple sits in the overlap.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Natural numbers, Integers and Negative numbers**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting only the outer circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
practice.solution: Every natural number is an integer → inside. −1 is a negative integer, but −½ is negative and not an integer → Negative numbers cut Integers. No natural number is negative → it stays away from the inner circle. Answer: **one circle inside a second; the third intersecting only the outer circle**.
practice.shortcut: Test −1 and −½; the third circle can touch the outer circle only.
